_comment: Short articles about changes and news on the network. `official` is maintainer-written; `community` is published from submissions the same way ideas are — nothing reaches either file automatically. An `image` is optional: `src` is a path under media/updates/, `alt` describes it for anyone who cannot see it, `focus` is a CSS object-position keeping the important part in frame when the card crops it, and `credit` names whoever the photograph belongs to. Do not publish a third-party photograph without a credit and the right to use it.

updates.title: We've asked West Sussex for its bus planning records
updates.author: Connor R
updates.summary: A Freedom of Information request asks West Sussex County Council where its bus money goes, what it has discussed with Brighton & Hove, and who uses the Discovery ticket. The council replied on 26 October, 11 working days late.

image.alt: An open copy of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, with the royal coat of arms above the title and the opening words of the Act below it.
image.credit_note: The site owner confirmed on 18 October 2026 that this photograph is free to use. The photographer, licence name and source link are not recorded; if the licence turns out to require attribution, put the credit in `credit`. Not guessed here.

updates.body:
On 13 September we sent West Sussex County Council a Freedom of Information request about buses across the boundary between Adur and Brighton & Hove. The council acknowledged it the same day as reference FOI/13765. The Act gives it 20 working days to answer, which runs to 9 October.

Most of what this site says about the gap either side of Portslade comes from the published timetable: how many buses are scheduled, where they stop, which tickets cover them. That shows what the network looks like. It can't show why. A timetable doesn't record how the council spends its bus funding, or whether anyone has sat down with Brighton & Hove to plan a route that crosses the line.

So we asked for four things.

Where the money goes. Bus Service Improvement Plan and Local Authority Bus Grant funding since April 2022, broken down across the seven districts and boroughs of West Sussex, and the subsidy paid each year to supported services on the A259 coast road or on routes that cross into Brighton & Hove. If Adur gets less than its neighbours, that should show up here.

Any plans to run buses across the boundary, at whatever stage they reached: proposed, under review, rejected or planned. That includes anything an operator has put forward about running further west than Shoreham, or further east into Brighton.

Minutes and agendas from the Enhanced Partnership board and forum since January 2023, wherever cross-boundary travel, the coastal corridor or working with Brighton & Hove came up. The Enhanced Partnership is where the council and the operators agree how local buses run. If a joined-up plan with Brighton & Hove were being discussed anywhere, it would be there.

How many Discovery tickets are sold on West Sussex services, and whether the council knows how many people use them to get to work rather than for days out. It is the only ticket every operator on this coast accepts, but it is priced and sold as a leisure rover. We want to know whether anyone is tracking who ends up relying on it.

We don't know yet what will come back. Some of this may not be held in the form we asked for, and a request can be cut down if answering it would cost more than the Act allows. We asked the council to tell us how to narrow it if that happens, rather than refuse it outright.

The request and every reply to it are public on WhatDoTheyKnow, so you can read the council's answer as soon as it lands. We'll write up what it says here, and the boundary evidence on the Route view shows the timetable figures it will be read against.

updates.title: Single fares drop to £2 in January
updates.summary: The national cap on a single bus fare falls from £3 to £2 from 1 January 2027.

image.alt: The destination display on the front of a double-decker bus reading “£2 Fare Cap”.
image.credit_note: The site owner confirmed on 18 October 2026 that this photograph is free to use. The photographer, licence name and source link are not recorded; if the licence turns out to require attribution, put the credit in `credit`. Not guessed here.

updates.body:
It matters more here than the headline suggests. Crossing the Worthing/Brighton DayRider boundary does not by itself require two buses, because the 700 runs straight through it. But a ticket boundary is where the day-ticket options stop covering you, so the fare cap is what keeps that journey at £6 return today and £4 from January. That is cheaper than every day ticket covering the same trip, which tells you something about how those zones are drawn.

Where two buses are needed, Lancing to Brighton say, it is two singles each way: £12 return today, £8 once the cap drops.

The Ticket view journey checker prices singles alongside day tickets, so you can see which is cheaper for a given trip.

updates.title: Stagecoach moves to Ticketer, the same system B&H already runs
updates.summary: Once Stagecoach's rollout, due to begin in September, reaches this coast, both major operators here will run the same ticketing platform. That weakens the technical objection to accepting each other's tickets; it does not settle the commercial one.

image.alt: A contactless bank card held against a blue Ticketer reader on a bus, the driver’s console display above it reading “Ticketer smart ticketing”.
image.credit_note: The site owner confirmed on 18 October 2026 that this photograph is free to use. The photographer, licence name and source link are not recorded; if the licence turns out to require attribution, put the credit in `credit`. Not guessed here.

updates.body:
Stagecoach has appointed Ticketer as its supplier of ticketing and real-time information technology, deploying the detachable TK300 ticket machine across its fleet. The national rollout was due to begin in September 2026. The platform combines electronic ticketing, vehicle location and real-time information in one system.

Every Brighton & Hove bus already runs Ticketer. So once the rollout reaches this coast, the two operators that meet at Shoreham, where Brighton & Hove's network ends and Stagecoach's carries on west, will be issuing and reading tickets on the same equipment from the same supplier.

What this changes is the strength of one argument, not the state of the network. Mutual ticket acceptance has always carried a technical objection: two different ticketing systems, two sets of hardware. A shared supplier makes that objection harder to sustain.

It does not by itself make acceptance possible. A rollout beginning in September is not the same as local completion, and common equipment is not the same as interoperable products or an agreed way of splitting the revenue between operators. Those are commercial decisions, and nobody has announced them. We are asking for them; we are not reporting them as done.

links.label: Stagecoach selects Ticketer for nationwide ticketing (routeone)

updates.title: Western Road closed: Brighton & Hove diversions until 6 November
updates.summary: Roadworks close Western Road between Holland Road and Montpelier Road until 6 November. Most Brighton & Hove routes through Hove are diverted, and Norfolk Square, Brunswick Place and Montpelier Road (Waitrose) are not served.
updates.author: Connor R
updates.body:
Western Road in Hove is closed between Holland Road and Montpelier Road for roadworks until 6 November, and more than a dozen Brighton & Hove routes are on diversion. The map already shows the three stops that are not served, crossed out on every bus's list of stops, with the nearest stops still in use. This is Brighton & Hove's notice in full:

"Due to roadworks on Western Road, we will be unable to serve all stops between Waitrose and Palmeira Square.

All Routes except 1X, 2 and 46 towards Hove will be on diversion via Montpelier Road, Davigdor Road and Holland Road to resume full route from Palmeira Square.

Routes 1X, 2 and 46 will be on diversion via Montpelier Road, Montpelier Place and Holland Road to resume full route from Palmeira Square.

Route 71A, is only affected in 1 direction towards Mile Oak.

All routes towards Brighton will be on diversion via Holland Road, Lansdowne Road and Montpelier Road to resume full route from Waitrose.

During this time, we will be unable to serve:

Norfolk Square

Brunswick Place

Montpelier Road (Waitrose)

All stops on the diversion routes will be served.

Please allow extra time for travelling during these times."

Journey times measured on these routes while the diversion runs will be longer than usual, and we have recorded the dates so they can be set apart from the rest of our figures.

image.alt: Shopfronts along Western Road in Brighton, including a Shelter charity shop on the corner, with people crossing the road beside a bus lane.

updates.title: What West Sussex told us about bus funding, and what it held back
updates.author: Connor R
updates.summary: Adur got £2.87 per resident from the council's spending on real-time bus stop displays, under half Worthing's £5.84. The council withheld its cross-boundary plans and partnership minutes, and holds no figures on the Discovery ticket.
updates.body:
West Sussex County Council answered our Freedom of Information request on 26 October, 11 working days after the legal deadline. It sent figures for some of its Bus Service Improvement Plan (BSIP) spending, withheld everything about plans for buses across the boundary with Brighton & Hove, and said it holds no information on the Discovery ticket. Here is what it told us, and what it didn't.

Real-time departure displays at bus stops are the one item the council broke down by district. Of £4.23 million spent on them from BSIP funds, Adur received £186,048. That is £2.87 for each person living in Adur, against £5.84 in Worthing and £4.62 across West Sussex. Adur is home to 7.1% of the county's residents and received 4.4% of the money. Only Crawley received less per resident, at £1.81.

For the rest of its BSIP spending, the council says it can't tell us where the money went. BSIP and Local Authority Bus Grant funding is "not allocated or committed on a geographical basis", and spending on bus stops and bus priority "is not tracked by District or Borough". The council tried to work it out from its own map of BSIP schemes and couldn't; doing it by hand would mean costing each site one at a time. As things stand, nobody can say from the council's records whether Adur has had a fair share.

The council did send a spreadsheet of BSIP support for bus services: 24 entries, worth £7.65 million up to September 2026. Four of them run into Brighton & Hove, and together they received £550,408, or 7.2% of the total. Only one of the four serves Adur: the N700 night bus between Brighton and Durrington, which has received £86,250 since April 2025. It is also the only entry under the spreadsheet's own heading for the A259 coast road.

That matters for our objective of a night service that goes west. We have asked for more night buses from Brighton into Adur and Worthing, and for ordinary day tickets to be valid on the N700. The N700 now receives public money through the council, so the council is one of its funders. We don't know whether that support came with any conditions on fares, and we'll ask.

BSIP has also paid for £8.66 million of building work across the county. £4.19 million went on bus stops, shelters and laybys, and £1.24 million on giving buses priority at traffic lights; the reply didn't say where. The two schemes it named are both in Crawley: the Manor Royal bus lane (£1.97 million) and the Western Boulevard junction and bus lane (£1.26 million). The council's 2024 bus plan does say where the traffic light work is aimed: its signal upgrades are "Focussing on improved journey times for the Coastliner Route 700", the bus along the coast road through Adur.

Together, the figures in the reply come to £20.54 million: £7.65 million for bus services, £4.23 million for displays and £8.66 million for other building work. The council's BSIP page says the government has awarded it £28.85 million: £17.4 million in 2022, £2.2 million in 2023 and £9.25 million in 2025. The reply doesn't account for the other £8.31 million. The council's 2024 bus plan lists BSIP spending the reply didn't itemise, including the fare discount for 16 to 20-year-olds, promoting bus travel, staff time to run the partnership and support for commercial bus services, so part of the gap is likely to be spending the reply left out. Some may also be 2025 money not yet spent. We'll ask the council for a full account.

We also asked for the subsidy paid each year to services on the coast road or into Brighton & Hove. The spreadsheet gives BSIP money only, mostly as one total per service. It has nothing from the council's own budget for the bus services it contracts, which its BSIP page describes as separate from the BSIP support.

On the questions that matter most for joining up the coast, the council released nothing. We asked about plans for routes across the boundary, at any stage from proposed to rejected, and for Enhanced Partnership minutes where cross-boundary travel or working with Brighton & Hove came up. The council withheld both under section 43 of the Freedom of Information Act, saying the information "is a trade secret" and that releasing it would harm the commercial interests of "the authority and/or contractor". Its reply confirms it holds information relevant to our request, but not what these records say.

The council holds no figures on Discovery ticket sales, and no analysis of whether people use the ticket to get to work. The Discovery ticket is the only ticket every operator on this coast accepts, and the council isn't tracking who relies on it.

We don't think plans and meeting minutes are trade secrets, and parts of the request went unanswered, so we intend to ask the council for an internal review. We'll publish what comes back.

How we worked out the display figures: each district's spending is the council's own figure from its reply. We divided it by that district's population in the Office for National Statistics' mid-2024 estimates (Adur 64,889; Worthing 113,866; West Sussex 915,037). The figures cover spending to date, not one year. They don't show how many displays each district got or how many bus stops it has, and a district with fewer stops would need fewer displays. The council's reply and spreadsheet are public on WhatDoTheyKnow.

Updated 27 October 2026: added what the council's 2024 bus plan says about where its traffic light work is aimed, and the spending it lists that the reply didn't.
